summary: This guide from the Refero design skill lists the patterns that make an interface look AI-generated and gives a rule for each. The nine named tells are indigo/violet accents, cards everywhere, dark mode by default, calm editorial serif on autopilot, emoji as icons, decorative left accent stripes, averaging strong references into a safe middle, changing what a style token means, and faking or dropping image-led media. It then lists generic typography, color, layout and visual symptoms, the intentional alternatives, a pre-ship checklist and six litmus tests (card, image, brand, copy, identity, editorial). For a design system it supplies defaults (light mode, no indigo, cards only for interaction) and a stance that every choice must be justified for this specific product.
key_ideas: AI interfaces converge on the same patterns because models optimize for safe and average choices.
Indigo/violet is the most recognisable fingerprint of AI-generated design; avoid it unless the brand requires it.
Cards are justified only when the container is the thing the user interacts with.
Light mode is the baseline unless the brief asks for dark.
The calm editorial look (cream, big serif, one italic word, earth tones) is fine for content-led brands but slop elsewhere.
A colored side stripe should mean something such as status, priority, owner or selection.
Synthesis means picking one primary reference and keeping its signature traits, not averaging references.
A token's role is part of the token; do not reuse a CTA-only accent as a background.
Keep the media role of image-led references with real assets, simple code-native graphics or honest placeholders.
Use one dominant color plus a sharp accent rather than an even spread of color.
Run litmus tests before shipping, such as removing a card's border, shadow, background and radius to see if anything breaks.
Every design choice should be explainable with a reason specific to this project.

claims.claim: AI models default to indigo/violet because training data is saturated with Tailwind's indigo and LLMs optimize for the average.
Cards are the second most common AI-slop pattern.
Dark-by-default is an AI fingerprint just like indigo.
claims.evidence: THE #3 TELL: DARK MODE BY DEFAULT

claims.claim: Newer models avoid indigo by switching to a calm editorial template of warm ivory, oversized serif and earth tones.
claims.evidence: THE #4 TELL: CALM EDITORIAL SERIF ON AUTOPILOT

claims.claim: Standard emoji immediately signal that a design is AI-generated.
In shipped products the left accent stripe is reserved for callouts, alerts, active items, status and priority.
AI models often do real research and then average strong references into the safest middle point.
Agents collapse image-led references into text and CSS decoration because they cannot generate the image, losing the style's main carrier.
claims.evidence: THE #9 TELL: FAKE GRAPHICS OR TEXT-ONLY COLLAPSE

claims.claim: AI over-writes copy; real designers edit down.

quotes: A token's role is part of the token. Preserve it or do not use it.
Serif fonts and earthy palettes are not banned. Autopilot "calm editorial" is.
Synthesis means choosing and adapting, not finding the least risky intersection.

rules.rule: Do not use an indigo/violet accent unless the brand explicitly requires it; pick blue, teal or a brand color instead.
rules.why: Indigo/violet is the universal fingerprint of AI-generated design.
rules.evidence: RULE: NEVER use indigo/violet unless the brand explicitly requires it.

rules.rule: Default to no cards; group content with sections, columns, dividers or media blocks, and use a card only when the container is a clickable item, form or expandable panel.
rules.why: AI wraps everything in rounded shadowed boxes because it feels safe; real designers use cards sparingly.

rules.rule: Remove a card if taking away its border, shadow, background and radius does not hurt interaction or understanding.
rules.why: Then it is not really a card.

rules.rule: Use light mode unless the brief explicitly asks for dark.
rules.why: Dark mode is a deliberate brand choice, and dark-by-default is an AI fingerprint.
rules.evidence: RULE: Unless the brief explicitly asks for dark — use light mode.

rules.rule: Do not use the warm ivory + oversized serif + earth-tone 'calm editorial' pattern unless you can say why this product needs an editorial voice, a serif display face and earth tones, and which references support it.
rules.why: It suits editorial, cultural, hospitality or fashion brands but is AI slop on dev tools, SaaS, fintech or dashboards.
rules.evidence: RULE: Do not use the calm editorial serif + earth-tone pattern

rules.rule: Do not swap one word or short phrase of a headline into a different serif, italic or color just to add 'taste'; create distinction through layout, scale, weight, media or a source-backed color role.
rules.why: The decorative one-word treatment is now a common AI default.

rules.rule: Never use emoji as icons unless the user explicitly asks; use an icon library, Unicode symbols or SVG.
rules.why: Emoji make a design look cheap, unfinished and AI-generated.
rules.evidence: RULE: Never use emoji unless the user explicitly asks for them.

rules.rule: Use a colored side accent stripe only when it communicates status, priority, owner or selection, never as decoration.
rules.why: If you cannot say in one word what the color means, it is decoration.

rules.rule: When references conflict, pick one primary direction and keep its signature traits; let secondary references add only 1-2 specific details.
rules.why: Averaging turns bold references into the same safe cream-and-clay look.

rules.rule: Keep each token in the role its source gave it: do not turn a CTA-only accent into backgrounds or badges, or code syntax colors into UI accents.
rules.why: Changing what a token means is a failure mode; uniqueness should come from composition.

rules.rule: Preserve the media role of an image-led reference with a real asset, stock or generated image, a simple code-native graphic, or an intentional placeholder with fixed aspect ratio, art direction and alt/caption; never fake photos or complex art with CSS blobs.
rules.why: Collapsing image-led styles into text and CSS loses the style's main carrier.
rules.evidence: THE #9 TELL: FAKE GRAPHICS OR TEXT-ONLY COLLAPSE

rules.rule: Add letter-spacing to ALL CAPS and small text.
rules.why: Missing letter-spacing on all caps is a generic-design symptom.

rules.rule: Build a clear type hierarchy of 3-4 distinct levels, differentiated by weight and spacing as well as size.
rules.why: Same weight throughout and no display/body distinction look generic.

rules.rule: Use a dominant color plus one sharp accent instead of evenly distributed color.
rules.why: Perfectly even color distribution with no accent hierarchy looks generic.

rules.rule: Break the grid intentionally with one element, not everything.
rules.why: Visual tension comes from intentional asymmetry; perfectly symmetrical everything looks generic.

rules.rule: If the first viewport works fine without the hero image, make the image dominant or remove it.
rules.why: The image is too weak.

rules.rule: If deleting 30% of the copy improves the page, keep deleting.
rules.why: AI over-writes; real designers edit down.

rules.rule: If the brand disappears after hiding the nav, make it louder: a bigger logo, brand color in the hero, or distinctive typography.
rules.why: Hierarchy is too weak.

rules.rule: If the first viewport could belong to any other company, add the one detail that makes it unmistakably this brand.
rules.why: Branding is too weak.

rules.rule: If swapping the logo for a coffee shop, boutique hotel or literary magazine still leaves the hero plausible, make the visual language specific to the actual product.
rules.why: The design is probably generic calm editorial slop.

rules.rule: Do not use gradients that do not serve a function, or abstract blob backgrounds and generic 3D illustrations.
rules.why: They are listed as symptoms of generic design.

rules.rule: Make semantic colors actually semantic, and build the palette from references rather than defaults.
rules.why: Colors used outside their stated role, or chosen by default, read as generic.

decisions.question: What accent hue should the product use when there is no brand color?

options.name: Indigo/violet
options.effect: Reads as the default AI-generated look.
options.when: Only when the brand explicitly requires it.

options.name: Teal #0d9488
options.when: You want to stand apart from generic SaaS.

decisions.recommendation: Avoid indigo/violet; use a brand color, or blue or teal, because indigo is the fingerprint of AI design.

decisions.question: Should the default color mode be light or dark?

options.name: Light
options.when: The brief says nothing about color mode.

options.name: Dark
options.when: The brief explicitly asks for dark.

decisions.recommendation: Light unless the brief explicitly asks for dark.
decisions.evidence: THE #3 TELL: DARK MODE BY DEFAULT

decisions.question: How should content be grouped: cards or open layout?

options.name: Cards
options.effect: Rounded boxes with shadows around each group.
options.when: The container is a clickable item, form or expandable panel.

options.name: Sections, columns, dividers or media blocks

decisions.recommendation: No cards by default; cards only for interaction.

decisions.question: Which visual direction fits the product?

options.name: Calm editorial serif with earth tones
options.effect: Warm ivory, oversized serif headline, olive/clay/terracotta accents, airy spacing.
options.when: Publishing, culture, fashion, hospitality or other content-led brands.

options.name: A sharper product-specific direction
options.effect: Technical, utilitarian, high-contrast, image-led, data-dense, playful, industrial, clinical or luxury.
options.when: Dev tools, enterprise SaaS, fintech, dashboards and functional product UI.

decisions.recommendation: Choose the editorial direction only when product context and research justify it; otherwise choose a direction grounded in research.
decisions.evidence: THE #4 TELL: CALM EDITORIAL SERIF ON AUTOPILOT

decisions.question: When the needed image is unavailable, what should stand in for it?

options.name: Real or generated asset
options.effect: Keeps the reference's media role intact.
options.when: A screenshot, provided asset, stock or generated image is available.

options.name: Code-native primitive
options.when: Simple diagrams, icons, charts, code windows, grids or geometric patterns.

options.name: Intentional placeholder
options.effect: Fixed aspect ratio, art direction and alt/caption hold the composition honest.

options.name: Text-only or CSS blob fake
options.effect: Loses the style's main carrier and looks fake.

decisions.recommendation: Use a real asset first, a code-native primitive for simple graphics, and a placeholder only when nothing suitable exists.

process.detail: Review the design for indigo, default cards, dark default, autopilot editorial serif, emoji icons, decorative stripes, averaged references, token role drift and faked media.
Answer why the product needs an editorial voice, why a serif display face, why earth tones, and which references support it; if you cannot, pick a sharper direction.
When references conflict, choose one primary direction, preserve its signature traits, and let secondary references contribute 1-2 details.
Give each reference a role, for example one owns canvas and type, another the code window, another the primary CTA, and keep their rules.
Tick each item before shipping, including accent not indigo, cards justified, light mode, ALL CAPS letter-spacing and the screenshot test next to real products.
Apply the card, image, brand, copy, identity and editorial tests and fix what fails.

examples.visual_note: A dark workbench, an acid-yellow docs site, a saturated orange brand and a serif editorial page all collapse into the same warm cream canvas with muted clay accents.
An acid-yellow reserved for the primary CTA ends up as a section background; syntax colors leave the code window and become UI accents.
Swap the logo for a coffee shop, boutique hotel or literary magazine; if the hero still feels plausible, it is generic calm editorial slop.
3-column pricing because everyone does it versus 2-column pricing because the product has only 2 tiers.
A 4px colored bar on a card's left edge, acceptable only for callouts, alerts, active list items, status or priority.

caveats: Written as instructions for an AI agent using Refero's MCP research; several rules assume 'Refero research' is available.
The claim about why AI defaults to indigo (Tailwind training data) is the authors' explanation, not a measured finding.
Opinionated defaults (light mode, no cards) are framed as hard rules; they are the source's stance for avoiding generic output, not universal standards.
